# Representation and Kernel Modifications

Also called: Kernel Variants, Primitive Representation Extensions

## Overview
Representation and Kernel Modifications extend the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting primitive set to address specific limitations in geometry, memory, and visual fidelity. While standard 3DGS uses symmetric positive Gaussians for radiance fields, this family introduces negative coefficients for subtractive blending, neural-predicted attributes for memory efficiency, tangent-space constraints for surface coherence, alternative radial basis functions for convergence, and spatially-varying blur kernels for defocus modeling. These methods differ from [Base 3DGS Optimization](7549-base-3dgs-optimization.md) by altering the fundamental mathematical definition of the splat or its attribute generation, rather than just the training schedule or loss functions.

## Shared principles
The family shares the core differentiable rasterization pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting, where 3D primitives are projected to 2D, sorted by depth, and composited using alpha blending [Parent]. However, the specific parameterization of the primitive $G_i$ (mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, opacity $\alpha$, color $\mathbf{c}$) or the kernel function $K$ evaluating the density is modified. All variants maintain the ability to backpropagate photometric loss to the underlying parameters, whether they are explicit Gaussian attributes, neural network weights, or kernel coefficients.

## Subtopics

### [Negative Gaussian Splatting](9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md)
Negative Gaussian Splatting (NegGS) extends the primitive set to include Gaussians with negative color values, enabling subtractive color blending [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md]. Unlike standard 3DGS, which requires many components to approximate complex shapes, NegGS uses negative Gaussians to alleviate time complexity while improving the representation of shadows and rapid color transitions. It maintains a joint family $G_{NeGS} = G_{GS} \cup G_{-GS}$, where $G_{-GS}$ contains tuples with negative $c_i$ [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md]. The rendering equation is preserved: $C = \sum c_i \alpha_i \prod_{j < i} (1 - \alpha_j)$, allowing negative contributions [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md]. Initialization requires approximately 20% of Gaussians to be negative for optimal efficacy [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md]. It can be interpreted as using "Diff-Gaussians," formed by dividing the PDFs of two Gaussians, allowing approximation of structures like donuts [9152-negative-gaussian-splatting.md]. Choose this when modeling high-frequency elements, shadows, or complex nonlinear structures where standard additive blending is inefficient.

### [Scaffold-GS](9186-scaffold-gs.md)
Scaffold-GS replaces the explicit storage of Gaussian attributes with a neural representation driven by a voxel grid [9186-scaffold-gs.md]. It solves the problem of inefficient memory usage and poor initialization in sparse regions by predicting all primitive parameters (mean, covariance, opacity, color) from learnable features attached to voxel points, rather than storing them directly [9186-scaffold-gs.md]. It differs from standard 3DGS by decoupling the geometric scaffold (voxels) from the rendered primitives (Gaussians) [9186-scaffold-gs.md]. Choose this when memory efficiency is critical or when dealing with sparse initializations where explicit attribute storage is wasteful.

### [GeoGaussian](9187-geogaussian.md)
GeoGaussian is a training optimization strategy that improves geometric consistency and surface reconstruction quality by enforcing local surface geometry constraints [9187-geogaussian.md]. It addresses the lack of explicit geometric constraints in standard 3DGS by densifying primitives on the tangent plane of existing Gaussians and enforcing smoothness of geometric properties (e.g., normals) between neighboring Gaussians [9187-geogaussian.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings like Negative Gaussian Splatting (which focuses on subtractive color blending) and Scaffold-GS (which uses neural feature prediction) by explicitly modeling local surface geometry through tangent-space densification and geometric smoothness regularization [9187-geogaussian.md]. Choose this when high-fidelity surface reconstruction and geometric coherence are prioritized over pure photometric accuracy.

### [DARBF-Splatting](9911-darbf-splatting.md)
DARBF-Splatting replaces the standard Gaussian reconstruction kernels with Decaying Anisotropic Radial Basis Functions (DARBFs) [9911-darbf-splatting.md]. It solves the limitation of existing splatting methods being restricted to the exponential family, offering improved training convergence speed and reduced memory usage while maintaining comparable visual quality [9911-darbf-splatting.md]. Unlike standard 3DGS, which relies on the closed-form integration properties of Gaussians, DARBF-Splatting introduces a scalar correction factor $\psi$ to approximate this efficiency for non-exponential kernels (e.g., Half-Cosine, Inverse Multiquadric) [9911-darbf-splatting.md]. Choose this when faster convergence or specific kernel properties (like finite support) are desired.

### [Grid-based Blur Kernel](14244-grid-based-blur-kernel.md)
Grid-based Blur Kernels replace neural network-generated blur kernels with a set of learnable, spatially indexed 2D convolution kernels to model spatially-varying defocus in NeRF [14244-grid-based-blur-kernel.md]. Unlike methods that use MLPs to predict kernel weights per pixel, this approach indexes a fixed grid of kernels based on a precomputed sharpness map, allowing expressivity to scale with grid size without additional inference cost [14244-grid-based-blur-kernel.md]. It operates as a post-processing or joint optimization layer on top of the standard differentiable rendering pipeline [14244-grid-based-blur-kernel.md]. Choose this when modeling realistic depth-of-field effects with spatially varying defocus.

### Gaussian Shell Maps
Gaussian Shell Maps (GSMs) combine CNN-based generators with 3DGS to recreate virtual humans with sophisticated details such as clothing and accessories [S1]. This variant is particularly suited for animatable human reconstruction where high-frequency appearance details (like fabric folds) need to be captured beyond standard spherical harmonics.

### Gaussian Wrapping
Gaussian Wrapping reinterprets 3D Gaussian primitives as oriented probabilistic surface elements representing geometry only within an oriented half-space, allowing derivation of closed-form occupancy, vacancy, and normal fields for watertight mesh extraction [S2]. It models surface points with asymmetric primitives where the Gaussian models density decay on the outward-facing side, while the inward-facing side is considered fully occupied [S2]. It identifies geometric gaps where the oriented surface assumption is violated and densifies the representation to obtain a watertight shell of oriented primitives [S2]. It introduces a learnable oriented normal at each Gaussian element and defines an adapted attenuation formulation to enable closed-form expressions for normal and occupancy fields [S2]. It introduces a novel consistency loss and a dedicated densification strategy to enforce Gaussians to wrap the entire surface by closing geometric holes [S2]. It modifies the differentiable rasterizer to output depth as an isosurface of the continuous model [S2]. It uses Primal Adaptive Meshing for Region-of-Interest meshing at arbitrary resolution [S2]. Choose this when watertight mesh extraction and high-fidelity surface geometry are the primary goals.

## Background
The standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation [Parent] was introduced by Kerbl et al. (2023) [G]. Subsequent modifications arose to address specific weaknesses: NegGS [S1, S2] and DARBF [S1] explored alternative mathematical formulations for density and color blending; Scaffold-GS [S1] and GeoGaussian [S1] focused on geometric and memory efficiency; Grid-based Blur Kernels [S1] addressed optical effects; and Gaussian Wrapping [S2] and GSMs [S1] targeted surface reconstruction and human avatars. These developments reflect the broader trend of adapting 3DGS for specialized applications beyond static scene rendering.
